Living in Quzhou County on the North China Plain, there's really only one system that makes sense for me: winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same land. This rotation has been the backbone of farming here for generations, and with my education I understand why — it maximizes the use of the land across both seasons, the markets for both crops are reliable, and my family's knowledge is built around it. I have 5 mu of arable land.

For the winter wheat, I'll rotary-till before sowing in October. I'll use an improved variety — something like Jimai 22 or a newer regional release — not traditional seed, because I know the improved lines have better disease resistance and yield potential. I'll apply base fertilizer with phosphorus and potassium at sowing, then top-dress nitrogen at the jointing stage. Irrigation is critical here because Quzhou is water-limited: I'll irrigate at sowing if soil moisture is low, again at spring green-up, and at jointing. That's three irrigations. I'll spray herbicide in autumn and a fungicide/insecticide pass around heading.

After wheat harvest in June, I'll plant summer maize directly into the stubble — no-tillage to save time and protect soil moisture. I'll use a hybrid like Zhengdan 958 or Xianyu 335, which are dominant in this area. Summer rainfall covers most of the maize's water needs, but I'll irrigate once at silking if it's dry. Two pesticide passes — one for fall armyworm risk, one as needed.
